claims.text: The starting alloy is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
The starting alloy can be produced by conventional powder metallurgy and sintering.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 undergoes Cr/V-rich precipitation under irradiation.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 has a low but measurable irradiation-hardening response.
Adding approximately 1–2 at% carbon during processing will form a stable, finely dispersed population of tungsten carbide particles.
The tungsten carbide particles will occur at grain boundaries and within grains.
Carbides preferentially nucleate and grow at microstructural defects and boundaries.
Energetic-particle irradiation produces point defects, defect clusters, and localized compositional changes.
Phase boundaries and other sinks absorb irradiation-induced point defects and can limit defect clustering and irradiation hardening.
The tungsten carbide particles will act as preferential sinks for irradiation-induced point defects.
The tungsten carbide particles will capture migrating Cr and V atoms.
The carbide particles will serve as heterogeneous nucleation sites for Cr and V.
Defect absorption and Cr/V capture by the carbides will limit local solute supersaturation and prevent nucleation and growth of Cr/V-rich precipitates.
At approximately 8 dpa, the carbon-doped alloy will have a significantly reduced or absent volume fraction of Cr/V-rich precipitates relative to the unmodified alloy.
At approximately 8 dpa, carbon doping will preserve negligible irradiation-induced hardening.
Carbon-derived carbides will enhance sinterability and the mechanical integrity of bulk samples.
Carbon doping may improve ductility and bulk manufacturability.
The proposed intervention is applicable to energetic-particle irradiation at 500–600 °C up to approximately 8 dpa.
Sintering and post-irradiation annealing must avoid temperatures that cause excessive carbide coarsening.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says carbides are heterogeneous nucleation sites for Cr and V, which would ordinarily facilitate Cr/V-rich phase nucleation, while the mechanism says those same carbides prevent nucleation and growth of Cr/V-rich precipitates. No distinction between benign carbide-associated segregation and deleterious precipitation is supplied.
